planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed, in well-drained sandy cactus mix; provide a sturdy post or trellis at planting time since this vining cactus needs support from the start. In zone 10-11 plant out year-round; elsewhere grow in containers and bring indoors below 40F.

directions: Grow on a strong post-and-collar or trellis in full sun with excellent drainage; Vietnamese Jaina is a widely grown selection of the classic white-fleshed pitaya, valued for oval fruit that commonly reach a pound or more with mild, refreshing sweetness. It is self-fertile, unlike many white-flesh types that need a pollinator partner, so a single plant can set fruit reliably once mature. Flowers open for a single night and are best hand-pollinated near dusk for heavier fruit set. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-30s but suffer scale damage below that; wrap or move containers during hard freezes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit in the Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Pitaya
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Dragon Fruit Production

planting.note: Propagate only from stem cuttings — Bruni is a hybrid clone and does not come true from seed. Root cuttings in spring in fast-draining cactus mix and provide trellis support immediately; in zones 10-11 plant out once rooted, elsewhere grow in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter.

directions: Provide a sturdy post or arbor in full sun with sharply drained soil; Bruni is a hybrid pitaya bred by a German hobbyist, distinguished from ordinary dragon fruit by neon pink-purple stem tips and smaller, prolific green-skinned fruit with sweet white flesh. Because it carries stenopterus parentage it is self-sterile and needs a compatible undatus-type pollinator planted nearby or hand pollination with foreign pollen for fruit to set. The triangular stems are more slender and tender than standard undatus, so protect from wind and hard freezes below 35F. Its flowers, like other pitayas, open for one night only and are most reliably pollinated by hand in the evening.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Pitaya
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit in the Home Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Dragon Fruit Production

planting.note: Plant air-layered or grafted trees in spring once soil has warmed, in zone 9-10 set out March-May. Like other longans, Biew Kiew needs several weeks of cool, dry winter weather below roughly 60F to induce flowering, so keep irrigation minimal in winter. Protect young trees below 30F.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Biew Kiew is a highly regarded Thai longan cultivar prized for large, thin-skinned fruit with a small seed and exceptionally sweet, faintly floral, translucent flesh often described as richer than Kohala. It ripens later in the season than Kohala, typically late summer into early fall, which helps spread out the harvest window for growers who plant both. Like all longans it needs a period of cool, relatively dry winter weather to set flower buds, making zone 9 climates with real winter chill better suited to consistent bearing than frost-free zone 10-11 sites. Trees are vigorous and can bear heavily once established, usually beginning by their fourth or fifth year from a grafted or air-layered start.
sources: University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Longan Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Longan Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Rare Fruit Council International cultivar notes

planting.note: Set out grafted trees in late spring once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F; rambutan is far more cold-sensitive than lychee or longan and is only reliably field-grown in true tropical zone 11-12 conditions in the continental US. Grow in a large container that can be moved indoors in cooler climates.

directions: Plant in deep, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from wind; R134 is one of the principal commercial rambutan selections released by Malaysian breeding programs, valued for medium-sized round fruit with soft green-tipped spinterns, a high percentage of edible aril, and a good sugar-to-acid balance. Unlike lychee and longan, rambutan has essentially no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, humid conditions with no dry-season stress to fruit well, which limits reliable outdoor cultivation in the US to South Florida and Hawaii. Trees are large and need considerable room to reach full bearing size, typically beginning to fruit four to six years after planting a grafted specimen. Keep soil consistently moist — unlike many tropical fruit trees, rambutan is intolerant of drought stress at any stage of growth.
sources: University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Rambutan Production
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Rambutan Fact Sheet
Tropical Fruit Network (TFNet) — Rambutan Cultivars

planting.note: Set out grafted trees in late spring once night temperatures stay above 60F; provide wind shelter and mulch to conserve soil moisture. In marginal zones grow in a large container that can be sheltered when temperatures drop.

directions: Grow in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun protected from strong wind; Jitlee is a compact, heavy-bearing rambutan cultivar producing clusters of bright crimson, free-stone fruit, and is popular in Southeast Asian orchards for its reliable, intense flowering. It is a male-dominant flowering type best interplanted with a hermaphroditic cultivar such as Rongrien to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. Because it stays smaller than many other rambutan selections it can be planted more closely and is a good option for growers with limited space in true tropical climates. Like all rambutan, it has no meaningful cold tolerance and requires warm, humid, frost-free conditions to thrive.
sources: University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Rambutan Production
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Rambutan Fact Sheet
Tropical Fruit Network (TFNet) — Rambutan Cultivars

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after the last frost, in a warm, wind-sheltered site with excellent drainage. Young trees need frost protection down to 30F for the first few winters; mature trees tolerate brief light frost with some leaf and twig damage.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Sri Kembangan is a Malaysian carambola selection grown for elongated, deep orange-yellow fruit with thin, waxy skin and firm, very sweet, low-acid flesh that eats well fresh with few seeds. It is a smaller, more manageable tree than many carambola seedlings and can be kept to a compact size with regular pruning, making it well suited to home gardens and large containers. Flowering and fruiting occur over an extended season, with the heaviest crop from late summer through winter in warm climates. Fruit color and sugar content develop best with full sun exposure; trees in part shade tend to produce paler, more acidic fruit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Carambola Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Carambola
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Carambola Fact Sheet

planting.note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring in warm, well-drained soil; protect young trees from temperatures below 30F. Established trees tolerate brief light frost but fruit and young growth are damaged by cold.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hasya is the leading commercial sapodilla cultivar in Mexico, selected for extra-large, football-shaped fruit that can weigh close to a pound, with a reddish-brown blush through the grainy, malty-sweet flesh. The tree grows into a large, upright form and bears prolifically once mature, with fruit maturing over a long window from late fall through late spring in warm climates. Fruit must be harvested mature but firm and allowed to ripen off the tree for several days until it yields to gentle pressure, since sapodilla picked too green stays astringent with latex and never develops proper sweetness. Sapodilla is highly wind- and salt-tolerant and, once established, one of the most drought-resistant of the common tropical fruit trees.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sapodilla Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Sapodilla
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Sapodilla Fact Sheet

planting.note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring after frost danger passes, in well-drained soil in full sun. Protect young trees below 29F; established trees recover readily from light frost damage by resprouting.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Lucknow 49 (also sold as Sardar) is India's most widely planted commercial guava cultivar, selected for its round to ovate fruit with smooth, primrose-yellow skin and firm, sweet, aromatic white pulp with relatively few, soft seeds. The tree is notably vigorous and productive, with attractive smooth bark that flakes away in patches to reveal pink and green new bark beneath. It bears two main crops per year in subtropical climates and fruits nearly continuously in frost-free tropical conditions, making it a heavy, reliable producer for home orchards. Regular pruning after harvest encourages the flush of new growth on which guava fruit is borne, keeping trees productive and manageably sized.
sources: Central Institute for Subtropical Horticulture — Guava Cultivars of India
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Guava Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Guava Fact Sheet
